newsitem.title: SURINAM: Alcoa Suriname unit sees 10 pct output rise in '97.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa Suriname unit sees 10 pct output rise in '97.

text.p: Aluminum and alumina output at Aluminum Co of America's Suriname unit, Suralco, will rise 10 percent this year as the company recovers from a damaging strike in 1996, Suralco president said.
"I am expecting output for this year to be 10 percent higher than last year," Henk Ramdin told Reuters in an interview.

That would bring alumina output up from less than 4,400 tonnes per day last year to an average 4,700 tonnes per day in 1997. Aluminum output would rise from a a total of 30,000 tonnes in 1996 to 33,000 tonnes this year, he said.
Failure to reach agreement with Suralco's 2,200 workers on a new collective contract closed down nearly all operations for three weeks last June.

Negotiations for a new contract should start in November and be completed before the end of the year. But after a generous settlement last year and negligible inflation since, Ramdin expects few problems.
"We should be able to resist extraordinary wage increases," he said.
Suralco aims to gradually raise alumina output to 4,800 tonnes per day in 1998 and to 5,000 tonnes per day in 1999.

"At this point in time, there are no plans for a substantial increase (in output)," Ramdin said. "We see a creep to about 5,000 tonnes (per day), but to go beyond that would require a major capital investment."

Output from the small aluminum smelter at Paranam, about 20 miles (30 km) south of Paramaribo, is also unlikely to increase much beyond 35,000 tonnes per year due to limited power supplies from the Afobaka hydroelectric plant in central eastern Suriname.

Suralco is 60 percent owned by Alcoa and 40 percent by Australia's Western Mining Co. All its production is exported, with aluminum going to Europe, 75 percent of alumina also to Europe and the remaining 25 percent to the United States.
The company's exports account for more than 75 percent, or $300 million, of Suriname's total export earnings.
As well as its own bauxite mine at Paranam, Suralco holds a minority stake in the Biliton mine at Moengo, in eastern Suriname, which is controlled by South Africa's General Mining Union Corp.
Reserves at the two mines would last until 2011 and Suralco and Biliton have identified reserves at concession areas in other parts of the country which could be developed, Ramdin said.
The world's third largest bauxite exporter in the 1960s and early 1970s, Suriname remains among the top 10 world producers, he said.
